stem: A company's servers were each built by hand and no two are configured alike, leaving unknown security gaps. Which action would BEST create a consistent, secure starting point across the fleet?

options.text: Define a hardened baseline configuration and deploy all servers from it
options.rationale: A standardized hardened baseline gives every system a known-good, consistent, reduced-attack-surface starting state, directly addressing the inconsistency.

options.text: Patch each server whenever a vulnerability is announced
options.rationale: Reactive patching addresses individual flaws but does not create a consistent secure configuration across systems.

options.text: Increase the frequency of vulnerability scans
options.rationale: Scanning finds issues but does not establish or enforce a consistent secure baseline.

options.text: Require longer passwords on all servers
options.rationale: Stronger passwords are one setting; they do not standardize the overall configuration or reduce broad attack surface.

stem: A newly imaged server ships with several default services enabled, unused open ports, and a default administrator account. Which activity BEST describes remediating these to reduce attack surface?

options.text: System hardening
options.rationale: Removing unneeded services, closing unused ports, and disabling default accounts to reduce attack surface is the definition of hardening.

options.text: Load balancing
options.rationale: Load balancing distributes traffic and is unrelated to reducing a single system's attack surface.

options.text: Data classification
options.rationale: Data classification labels information by sensitivity; it does not reduce a system's exposed services.

options.text: Capacity planning
options.rationale: Capacity planning sizes resources for demand; it has nothing to do with removing insecure defaults.

stem: Six months after deployment, several servers no longer match their approved configuration due to undocumented ad-hoc changes by various admins. This condition is MOST accurately called what?

options.text: Configuration drift
options.rationale: Undocumented, gradual deviation from the approved baseline over time is precisely configuration drift.

options.text: A denial-of-service condition
options.rationale: A DoS is a loss of availability from attack or overload, not a deviation from a configuration baseline.

options.text: A zero-day vulnerability
options.rationale: A zero-day is an unknown, unpatched flaw, not the divergence of systems from their baseline.

options.text: Data remanence
options.rationale: Data remanence is residual data left on media after deletion, unrelated to configuration deviation.

stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes configuration management from change management?

options.text: Configuration management maintains the authoritative baseline of deployed state; change management governs how modifications to it are approved
options.rationale: CM defines and preserves what is deployed (the baseline), while change management controls the process for altering it — complementary but distinct disciplines.

options.text: They are two names for the same process
options.rationale: They are related but not identical; conflating them is a classic exam trap.

options.text: Change management defines the baseline and configuration management approves changes
options.rationale: This reverses the two roles; it is configuration management that owns the baseline.

options.text: Configuration management applies only to network devices
options.rationale: CM applies broadly to hardware, software, and settings, not just network gear.

stem: To ensure every new workstation is deployed in an identical, known-good secure state, which approach is BEST?

options.text: Build a hardened master image and deploy all workstations from it
options.rationale: A gold image captures a hardened baseline and reproduces it exactly across systems, ensuring consistency and known security posture.

options.text: Let each technician configure each machine manually from a checklist
options.rationale: Manual builds reintroduce human error and inconsistency, the very problem imaging solves.

options.text: Deploy machines with vendor defaults and fix issues as users report them
options.rationale: Shipping insecure defaults and reacting to complaints leaves systems exposed and inconsistent.

options.text: Ship machines unconfigured and let users self-install software
options.rationale: User self-configuration produces uncontrolled, inconsistent, and likely insecure states.

stem: Which of the following is a widely recognized standard used to define secure configuration baselines?

options.text: CIS Benchmarks
options.rationale: CIS Benchmarks (like DISA STIGs) provide consensus secure-configuration guidance used to build hardened baselines.

options.text: OSI model
options.rationale: The OSI model is a conceptual networking layer model, not a configuration hardening standard.

options.text: RAID levels
options.rationale: RAID levels describe disk redundancy schemes, not configuration hardening baselines.

options.text: TCP three-way handshake
options.rationale: The three-way handshake is a connection-establishment mechanism, unrelated to hardening standards.

stem: An organization frequently spins up new cloud servers and finds manual setup slow and error-prone, sometimes leaving systems misconfigured. Which practice would MOST improve consistency and security?

options.text: Automated provisioning from a defined, hardened baseline
options.rationale: Automated provisioning reproduces the approved secure configuration reliably, eliminating manual error and drift at deployment time.

options.text: Assigning setup to whichever admin is available
options.rationale: Ad-hoc manual setup is exactly the source of the inconsistency and errors described.

options.text: Documenting a longer manual runbook
options.rationale: A longer manual process still relies on error-prone human steps and does not guarantee consistency.

options.text: Waiting to configure servers until users complain
options.rationale: Reactive configuration leaves systems misconfigured and insecure in the interim.

stem: A critical vulnerability is announced for a specific software version. The security team cannot determine which of thousands of systems run that version. What should the organization address FIRST to solve this recurring problem?

options.text: Establish an accurate configuration inventory (CMDB) of deployed configuration items
options.rationale: Without an authoritative inventory of what is deployed, the team cannot identify affected systems; building that inventory is the foundational fix.

options.text: Buy a more expensive antivirus product
options.rationale: Antivirus does not tell you which software versions are installed across the fleet.

options.text: Increase the firewall's throughput
options.rationale: Firewall performance is irrelevant to knowing which systems run a vulnerable version.

options.text: Rotate all administrative passwords
options.rationale: Rotating passwords is unrelated to identifying which systems are affected by the vulnerability.

stem: In configuration management, what is a baseline?

options.text: A formally agreed reference configuration against which changes and drift are measured
options.rationale: A baseline is the documented, approved reference state used as the point of comparison for changes and drift.

options.text: The minimum bandwidth a network link must provide
options.rationale: That describes a network performance floor, not a configuration baseline.

options.text: The lowest privilege a user can be granted
options.rationale: That relates to least privilege, not a configuration baseline.

options.text: The maximum acceptable downtime for a system
options.rationale: That is closer to an availability metric, not a configuration baseline.

stem: Continuous monitoring detects that a production server has drifted from its approved baseline. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Remediate the server back to the approved baseline (or re-image it) through the change process
options.rationale: Restoring the system to its known-good baseline, via controlled change, corrects the drift and returns it to a secure, documented state.

options.text: Update the baseline to match whatever the server now is
options.rationale: Blindly adopting drifted, unreviewed settings as the new baseline legitimizes potentially insecure ad-hoc changes.

options.text: Ignore it because the server is still running
options.rationale: Running does not mean secure; unmanaged drift can conceal vulnerabilities and must be addressed.

options.text: Immediately decommission the server
options.rationale: Decommissioning a production server for drift is disproportionate; remediation to baseline is the appropriate response.

stem: What is the PRIMARY security objective of hardening a system before deployment?

options.text: To reduce the attack surface by removing unnecessary functionality and insecure defaults
options.rationale: Hardening's core aim is minimizing exposure — fewer running services, closed ports, and no default accounts mean fewer avenues to attack.

options.text: To increase raw processing speed
options.rationale: Hardening targets security, not performance optimization.

options.text: To add as many features as possible
options.rationale: Adding features increases attack surface, the opposite of hardening.

options.text: To make the system easier for anyone to access
options.rationale: Broadening access conflicts with hardening, which restricts unnecessary access.

stem: Which capability BEST allows an organization to detect when systems have quietly diverged from their approved configurations?

options.text: Continuous configuration monitoring against the baseline
options.rationale: Ongoing comparison of live configurations to the baseline is what surfaces drift so it can be remediated.

options.text: An annual physical inventory count
options.rationale: A yearly count of assets does not reveal configuration-level deviations that occur throughout the year.

options.text: A stronger perimeter firewall
options.rationale: A firewall filters traffic; it does not detect internal configuration drift.

options.text: More frequent password changes
options.rationale: Password rotation is unrelated to detecting configuration deviations from baseline.

stem: A hospital must deploy 500 identical, securely configured clinical workstations quickly. Which method BEST ensures they all start in the same hardened state?

options.text: Deploy from a single hardened gold image
options.rationale: A master hardened image reproduces the identical secure configuration across all 500 machines efficiently and consistently.

options.text: Have each department configure its own machines its own way
options.rationale: Decentralized manual configuration guarantees inconsistency and varying security postures.

options.text: Install the operating system defaults and skip hardening to save time
options.rationale: Skipping hardening leaves insecure defaults across all machines, a poor security outcome.

options.text: Let end users install whatever software they prefer
options.rationale: User self-configuration produces uncontrolled, non-uniform, and likely insecure builds.

stem: An auditor asks which process is responsible for maintaining the authoritative record of exactly what hardware, software, and settings are currently deployed. This is MOST directly the responsibility of which process?

options.text: Configuration management
options.rationale: Maintaining the authoritative deployed-state record (baselines, configuration items, inventory) is the defining role of configuration management.

options.text: Incident management
options.rationale: Incident management handles detection and response to events, not maintaining the deployed-state record.

options.text: Change management
options.rationale: Change management approves modifications; it relies on, but does not itself maintain, the authoritative configuration record.

options.text: Vulnerability management
options.rationale: Vulnerability management identifies and remediates weaknesses; it does not own the deployed-state baseline record.

stem: A DevOps team wants new environments to be created identically every time with no manual steps. Which practice BEST supports this goal from a configuration standpoint?

options.text: Automated provisioning that deploys systems from a defined configuration
options.rationale: Automated, repeatable provisioning reproduces the exact intended configuration each time, eliminating manual variance.

options.text: A shared document listing setup steps for admins to follow by hand
options.rationale: Manual steps from a document still allow human error and inconsistency between environments.

options.text: Configuring the first environment and copying files ad hoc afterward
options.rationale: Ad-hoc copying is unreliable and does not guarantee identical, complete configurations.

options.text: Letting each engineer improvise the setup
options.rationale: Improvised setup produces divergent environments, the opposite of the stated goal.

stem: In configuration management, what is a configuration item (CI)?

options.text: Any hardware, software, or setting tracked under configuration management
options.rationale: A CI is any component whose configuration is managed and recorded, typically in a CMDB.

options.text: A ticket requesting a password reset
options.rationale: A password-reset request is a service request, not a tracked configuration component.

options.text: A firewall log entry
options.rationale: A log entry is a record of an event, not a managed configuration component.

options.text: An employee's job title
options.rationale: A job title is HR data, not a hardware/software/setting under configuration control.

stem: A monitoring tool reports that many workstations have insecure settings not present in the approved image, apparently applied piecemeal by local admins. What is the MOST effective long-term fix?

options.text: Re-image or remediate systems back to the hardened baseline and restrict who can alter configurations
options.rationale: Restoring systems to the approved baseline and controlling change prevents recurring unauthorized drift, addressing root cause.

options.text: Manually undo each individual setting on each machine and hope it stays fixed
options.rationale: One-off manual fixes without controlling who can change configurations will drift again; it does not address the root cause.

options.text: Accept the current settings as the new normal
options.rationale: Accepting unreviewed insecure changes institutionalizes the risk rather than correcting it.

options.text: Turn off the monitoring tool to stop the alerts
options.rationale: Silencing the detection hides the problem instead of remediating the insecure drift.

stem: A team building its first secure server baseline wants an authoritative, consensus reference rather than inventing settings themselves. Which source is BEST to build from?

options.text: An established hardening standard such as CIS Benchmarks or DISA STIGs
options.rationale: Recognized hardening standards provide vetted, consensus configuration guidance that is stronger than ad-hoc, self-invented settings.

options.text: Whatever settings the loudest team member prefers
options.rationale: Personal preference is not an authoritative, vetted hardening reference.

options.text: The vendor's default out-of-box configuration
options.rationale: Vendor defaults are typically insecure and are what hardening is meant to correct, not a secure reference.

options.text: A random configuration copied from a public forum post
options.rationale: Unvetted forum configurations lack authority and may introduce insecure or incorrect settings.

stem: As part of the configuration lifecycle, a server is being retired. From a security perspective, what is MOST important during deprovisioning?

options.text: Securely sanitize its storage and remove it from the inventory before disposal
options.rationale: Sanitizing media prevents data remanence exposure and updating inventory keeps the CMDB accurate as the system leaves the lifecycle.

options.text: Leave the system powered on in case it is needed later
options.rationale: Leaving a retired system running maintains attack surface and does not securely close out the asset.

options.text: Simply unplug it and leave the disks intact in storage
options.rationale: Intact disks risk data remanence if the media is later reused or stolen; sanitization is required.

options.text: Delete the inventory record but keep the disk untouched
options.rationale: Removing the record without sanitizing leaves sensitive data recoverable and the disposal untracked.

stem: Why does CISSP treat a well-maintained configuration baseline as foundational to operational security?

options.text: Because you cannot reliably secure, patch, or audit systems whose actual state you do not accurately know
options.rationale: An authoritative baseline provides the known state on which patching, auditing, and anomaly detection all depend.

options.text: Because baselines eliminate the need for any firewalls
options.rationale: Baselines complement, but do not replace, network controls like firewalls.

options.text: Because a baseline guarantees no vulnerabilities will ever exist
options.rationale: Baselines reduce and standardize risk but cannot guarantee the absence of all vulnerabilities.

options.text: Because baselines make user training unnecessary
options.rationale: Configuration baselines address system state, not the human factors that training covers.
